lead: Light can be steered inside a fiber by bouncing it at the core–cladding boundary. The core carries a higher refractive index than the cladding. When a ray strikes the boundary steeply enough, the boundary acts like a mirror. This is total internal reflection. It keeps the light in the core over long distances, so a transmitter can launch power into a narrow input cone and a receiver at the far end still gets signal. The same idea appears in endoscopes, optical sensors and chip waveguides.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the source–fiber–detector picture and the meaning of a core and cladding.

sections.h3: Refractive index and the critical angle

blocks.text: Refractive index n is the ratio of light speed in vacuum c to light speed in a material v: n = c/v. It has no unit. A larger n means slower light. In a step-index fiber the core has index n1 and the cladding has index n2, with n1 > n2. The medium outside the fiber has index n0; for air n0 = 1.

At a flat boundary between two materials, Snell's law links the angles: n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. Here θ1 is the angle in the first material measured from the normal, and θ2 is the angle in the second material measured from the same normal. The normal is the line perpendicular to the boundary.

When light goes from the denser core to the rarer cladding (n1 > n2), it bends away from the normal: θ2 > θ1. Increase θ1 and θ2 reaches 90° first. That value is the critical angle θc. Put θ2 = 90° in Snell's law: n1 sin θc = n2 × 1, so θc = sin⁻¹(n2/n1). For θ1 > θc there is no real refracted angle. All the light reflects back into the core. This is total internal reflection, TIR.

blocks.where: θc is the critical angle measured from the normal; n1 is the core refractive index; n2 is the cladding refractive index; n1 > n2.

sections.h3: From the end face to the acceptance cone

blocks.text: Most rays we draw are meridional rays: they pass through the fiber axis. A meridional ray enters the flat end face from air at angle θ0 to the fiber axis. The normal to that end face is the axis itself, so θ0 is also the angle of incidence. Snell's law at the end face is n0 sin θ0 = n1 sin θr, where θr is the ray angle inside the core, measured from the axis.

Inside the core the ray travels in a straight line until it hits the core–cladding boundary. The normal at that side boundary is radial. The angle of incidence at the side boundary is therefore 90° − θr. TIR needs 90° − θr > θc, or θr < 90° − θc.

The largest launch angle that still satisfies this is the acceptance angle θa. At the limit, θr = 90° − θc. Use Snell's law at the end face: n0 sin θa = n1 sin(90° − θc) = n1 cos θc = n1√(1 − sin²θc) = n1√(1 − (n2/n1)²) = √(n1² − n2²). For air outside, n0 = 1, so sin θa = √(n1² − n2²). The acceptance angle is the half-angle of the cone of rays that the fiber accepts. Numerical aperture is NA = sin θa; Chapter 1.3 treats it fully and adds skew rays.

blocks.where: θa is the acceptance angle in the outside medium; n0 is the outside refractive index; n1 and n2 are core and cladding indices.

blocks.text: Use the acceptance cone when you couple a source to a fiber. An LED or laser must sit inside the cone for its rays to be guided. A wider cone, meaning larger n1² − n2², accepts more rays. That helps coupling but usually means a larger core and more modes, which can spread the pulse; see Unit 2, Intermodal dispersion. The cone also explains alignment: tilt the fiber or the source beyond θa and launched power falls.

Only rays that are meridional and inside the cone are covered by this simple picture. Rays that miss the axis, called skew rays, follow helical paths and have a different bound condition; see Chapter 1.3. The step-index profile used here has a sudden index jump; Chapter 1.5 shows how grading the index changes ray paths. For a short link, this ray test is enough to decide whether a launched ray stays in the core.

figure.caption: A ray reaching the core–cladding boundary is tested against the critical angle. The upper branch is guided by total internal reflection; the lower branch leaves the core.

spec.title: Total internal reflection decision
spec.aria: A ray at the core–cladding boundary is compared with the critical angle; if the angle is larger, the ray stays in the core by total internal reflection, otherwise it refracts out.

examples.question: A step-index fiber has core index n1 = 1.50 and cladding index n2 = 1.45. The outside medium is air, n0 = 1. Find the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary, the numerical aperture, and the acceptance angle.
steps: Numerical aperture NA = √(n1² − n2²) = √0.1475 = 0.3841. With n0 = 1, NA = sin θa = 0.3841.
examples.answer: The critical angle is 75.2°, the numerical aperture is 0.384, and the acceptance angle is 22.6°.
examples.check:
import math
n1, n2, n0 = 1.50, 1.45, 1.0
theta_c = math.degrees(math.asin(n2/n1))
NA = math.sqrt(n1**2 - n2**2)
theta_a = math.degrees(math.asin(NA/n0))
print(round(theta_c, 1))
print(round(NA, 3))
print(round(theta_a, 1))

traps: Use n2/n1 for the critical angle, not n1/n2. Since n2 < n1, sin θc is less than 1.
TIR needs light to travel from the higher-index core to the lower-index cladding. If n2 > n1, no TIR occurs at that boundary.
Measure angles from the normal, not from the surface. A ray 70° from the boundary surface is only 20° from the normal.
The acceptance angle is measured in the outside medium, usually air, not inside the core. With n0 ≠ 1, use sin θa = √(n1² − n2²)/n0.
Do not call θc the acceptance angle. θc is inside at the core–cladding boundary; θa is at the input face.

quiz.q: State the two conditions for total internal reflection at a core–cladding boundary.
quiz.a: Light must travel from the higher-index core to the lower-index cladding (n1 > n2), and the angle of incidence measured from the normal must exceed the critical angle (θ > θc).

quiz.q: Why must the core index n1 be greater than the cladding index n2 for a step-index fiber?
quiz.a: With n1 > n2, light going from core to cladding bends away from the normal. A real critical angle exists, and rays above it reflect back into the core. If n2 > n1, light bends toward the normal and TIR does not occur at that boundary.

quiz.q: A step-index fiber has n1 = 1.48 and n2 = 1.46. Air is outside (n0 = 1). Find the critical angle and the acceptance angle.
A meridional ray enters from air at 25° to the fiber axis. The fiber has n1 = 1.50 and n2 = 1.45. Is the ray guided? Use the acceptance angle from the worked example.
quiz.a: The acceptance angle is 22.6°. The launch angle 25° is larger than 22.6°, so the ray is outside the acceptance cone and is not guided. Equivalently, inside the core θr = sin⁻¹(sin25°/1.50) ≈ 16.4°, so the side-boundary incidence is 90° − 16.4° = 73.6°, which is below θc = 75.2°; the ray refracts out.

quiz.q: Why is the acceptance angle measured in the medium outside the fiber rather than inside the core?
quiz.a: The acceptance angle describes the cone of rays that a source can launch into the fiber from the outside medium. Refraction at the end face changes the angle inside the core, so the inside angle is not the launch angle. The outside index n0 appears in n0 sin θa = √(n1² − n2²).

quiz.q: Define a meridional ray and the critical angle.
quiz.a: A meridional ray is a ray whose path passes through the fiber axis. The critical angle θc is the angle of incidence, measured from the normal, at which the refracted ray just grazes the boundary at 90°; for core-to-cladding incidence, sin θc = n2/n1.

quiz.q: The same fiber has n1 = 1.50 and n2 = 1.45, but it is now in water with n0 = 1.33. Find the acceptance angle in water.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ray theory is an approximation that works when the core diameter is many wavelengths. Real single-mode fibers need mode theory, as in Chapter 1.4. Ray tracing is still used for plastic optical fibers, illumination guides, endoscopes and short links. Search for 'meridional ray launch condition' and 'step-index fiber ray tracing' to go further.
